title: A Future and a Hope
subtitle: Jeremiah in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Jeremiah is the weeping prophet, called before he was born and sent to a city that would not listen. His book is full of plain, strange things: an almond branch in winter, a cracked cistern beside a running spring, a linen belt buried by a river, a potter bent over his wheel, two baskets of figs, a field bought while the army waits outside the walls, a scroll burned one piece at a time, and a rope let down into the mud with a bundle of rags. And in the middle of all the sorrow, a letter to the exiles about houses and gardens, and a promise of a new covenant written on the heart.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in five parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The hard chapters are told gently, through a dry cistern, a ruined belt and bronze pomegranates carried away, rather than the violence itself, because Jeremiah wept over them too.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the book of Jeremiah alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.lightHint: Near 'at the gate' (Jeremiah 7:1–23) in Part 2: Balm in Gilead

parts.lightHint: Near 'the potter’s house' (Jeremiah 18:1–6) in Part 3: The Potter’s House

parts.lightName: Light of Written on the Heart
parts.lightHint: Near 'everlasting' (Jeremiah 31:3–4) in Part 4: Written on the Heart

parts.title: Rags and Ropes

paintings.title: before
paintings.epigraph: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.”
paintings.poem:
before your name.
before your first breath.
before anyone had counted
your fingers and toes—

you were known.

not planned like a building,
drawn on a wall.
known,
the way a friend is known.

whatever you think
you have to earn,
it was never
the first thing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Jeremiah 1:4–5: “whatever you think you have to earn, it was never the first thing”?

paintings.title: only a child
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.”
paintings.poem:
i don't know how to speak,
he said.
i'm only a child.

God didn't argue
about his age.

he said:
don't be afraid.
i am with you.

then he reached out
and touched his mouth.

the words were never
going to be his.
only the courage
to open it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the quiet centerpiece of “only a child”: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “only the courage to open it”?

paintings.title: the almond branch
paintings.epigraph: “I see a branch of an almond tree.”
paintings.poem:
what do you see, Jeremiah?

just a branch.
an almond branch.

the first tree in the land
to wake up
while every other tree
is still asleep.

you have seen well,
God said.
i am watching too.

over every word
i have spoken—
awake,
before anyone else is.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “over every word i have spoken— awake, before anyone else is.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Jeremiah 1:11–12 right now?

paintings.title: the kindness of your youth
paintings.epigraph: “I remember for you the kindness of your youth, the love of your weddings”
paintings.poem:
before the scolding,
a memory.

i remember, God says,
how you followed me
through a land
no one had ever planted.

no fields.
no houses.
just the two of us
and a road in the sand.

the first thing he wants you to know
about his sorrow

is how much
he loved you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Jeremiah 2:1–3, grace meets us right beside the quiet centerpiece of “the kindness of your youth”: how does the closing thought—“the first thing he wants you to know about his sorrow is how much he loved you”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: broken cisterns
paintings.epigraph: “they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters”
paintings.poem:
two mistakes,
God says.

first,
you walked away
from a running spring.

then you spent your strength
cutting a hole in the rock
to hold rain.

and it cracked.

the saddest part
isn't the thirst.

it's all that work
for water
you could have
just been given.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “broken cisterns” (Jeremiah 2:13) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“it's all that work for water you could have just been given”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: return
paintings.epigraph: “Return, you backsliding children, and I will heal your backsliding.”
paintings.poem:
come back.

not
come back when you're better.
not
come back and explain.

come back,
and i will heal
the part of you
that keeps leaving.

the door he describes
is not locked.
he is standing
in it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Jeremiah 3:12–22)—where in your own home or work today does “the door he describes is not locked. he is standing in it” ring true?

paintings.title: the old paths
paintings.epigraph: “ask for the old paths, ‘Where is the good way?’ and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls.”
paintings.poem:
stand at the crossroads
for a minute.

don't hurry.

look for the path
worn smooth
by all the feet
that went before you.

ask it
where the good way is.

then walk in it,
and your soul
will do the thing
it's been asking for:

rest.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “then walk in it, and your soul will do the thing it's been asking for: rest.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: at the gate
paintings.epigraph: “Listen to my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people.”
paintings.poem:
he stood at the temple gate
while the crowds went in

saying,
the temple, the temple,
the temple of the Lord,

like a charm
to keep them safe.

and Jeremiah said:
it was never
about the stones.

it was always
one plain thing.

listen to me.
be my people.
i'll be your God.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “he stood at the temple gate while the crowds went in saying, the temple, the temple, the temple of the Lord, like a charm to keep them safe.” Looking through the lens of Jeremiah 7:1–23, what does it mean to discover that “be my people. i'll be your God”?

paintings.title: the stork
paintings.epigraph: “the stork in the sky knows her appointed times.”
paintings.poem:
the stork knows
when to come home.
the swallow knows.
the crane.

nobody teaches them.
something in them
turns toward the right place
at the right time.

and my people,
God says,
don't know
the way back to me.

it isn't a scolding.
it's a longing.

even the birds
remember.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the quiet centerpiece of “the stork” in this painting (Jeremiah 8:7)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: balm in Gilead
paintings.epigraph: “For the hurt of the daughter of my people, I am hurt.”
paintings.poem:
there was medicine
in Gilead.

everybody knew it.
a golden balm,
a healer close by.

so why,
the prophet asks,
isn't anyone
getting well?

he doesn't answer
from a distance.

her hurt
is my hurt,
he says.

the ones who carry the question
are the ones
who carry the wound.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the stone well in the heat of the day: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “the ones who carry the question are the ones who carry the wound”?

paintings.title: a spring of tears
paintings.epigraph: “Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a spring of tears”
paintings.poem:
he wished
he had more tears.

not fewer.
more.

enough to weep
day and night
for the people
he couldn't save.

some prophets thunder.
this one
cried.

and God
kept him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “a spring of tears” (Jeremiah 9:1) from “he wished he had more tears” to “this one cried. and God kept him”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: gently
paintings.epigraph: “Y ahweh, correct me, but gently”
paintings.poem:
i know my steps
aren't mine to steer,
he prayed.

so correct me.
i mean it.

but gently.

not in your anger—
i wouldn't be left.

it's one of the most honest prayers
in the Bible.

yes to the lesson.
and please,
remember
what i'm made of.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “gently” (Jeremiah 10:23–24) arrives at: “and please, remember what i'm made of.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: the linen belt
paintings.epigraph: “as the belt clings to the waist of a man”
paintings.poem:
God told him to wear
a linen belt,
then hide it
in a cleft of the rock
by the river.

many days later
he dug it up.
ruined.
good for nothing.

this is what pride does,
God said.

but listen
to what the belt was for:

i wanted you close,
the way a belt
holds to the one who wears it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Jeremiah 13:1–11: “but listen to what the belt was for: i wanted you close, the way a belt holds to the one who wears it”?

paintings.title: i ate them
paintings.epigraph: “Your words were found, and I ate them.”
paintings.poem:
everyone cursed him,
he said.
he didn't sit with the merrymakers.
he sat alone.

but there was this:

your words were found,
he said,
and i ate them.

like bread
to a hungry man.

the joy of my heart
wasn't in how it went.

it was in
whose name
i was called by.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the daily loaf broken in the hand: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “it was in whose name i was called by”?

paintings.title: by the waters
paintings.epigraph: “he will be as a tree planted by the waters”
paintings.poem:
heat comes.
a dry year comes.

the tree doesn't know
the forecast.

it just keeps
its roots in the river.

and its leaves stay green,
and the fruit keeps coming,
year of drought
or not.

trust
isn't a feeling
about the weather.

it's where
you put your roots.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “it's where you put your roots.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Jeremiah 17:7–8 right now?

paintings.title: the potter’s house
paintings.epigraph: “he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.”
paintings.poem:
go down to the potter's,
God said.

so he watched.

the pot was marred
in the potter's hands.

and the potter
didn't throw it away.
he began again.
another vessel,
whatever seemed good to him.

you are not
the mistake on the wheel.

you are the clay
still in his hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Jeremiah 18:1–6, grace meets us right beside the clay turning on the wheel: how does the closing thought—“you are the clay still in his hands”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: fire in my bones
paintings.epigraph: “there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones. I am weary with holding it in.”
paintings.poem:
everyone mocks me,
he said.
all day.

so i decided:
no more.
i won't mention him again.

and then—

it was like a fire
shut up
in my bones.

i tried to hold it in.
i couldn't.

he wanted to quit.
the word
didn't.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “fire in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:7–9) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“he wanted to quit. the word didn't”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: honest
paintings.epigraph: “Why did I come out of the womb to see labor and sorrow”
paintings.poem:
one line:
sing to the Lord!
he has rescued the poor.

the next:
why was i ever born?

he didn't tidy it up.
and neither did the Bible.

both prayers
are in there,
side by side.

so you can bring
the song
and the sorrow

to the same God
on the same day.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Jeremiah 20:13–18)—where in your own home or work today does “so you can bring the song and the sorrow to the same God on the same day” ring true?

paintings.title: the righteous Branch
paintings.epigraph: “I will raise to David a righteous Branch”
paintings.poem:
the shepherds
scattered the flock.

the kings
failed.

and God said:
i'll gather them myself.

and i'll raise
a Branch for David.

a king
who will actually do
what's right.

his name
will be
the Lord our righteousness.

a new shoot.
a promise.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “his name will be the Lord our righteousness. a new shoot. a promise.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: two baskets
paintings.epigraph: “I will give them a heart to know me”
paintings.poem:
two baskets of figs
at the temple steps.
one good.
one spoiled.

and the surprise:
the good figs
were the ones
already carried off to Babylon.

i have my eye on them,
God said.
for good.
i will give them
a heart to know me.

the ones who lost everything
were not lost
to him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “two baskets of figs at the temple steps.” Looking through the lens of Jeremiah 24:1–7, what does it mean to discover that “the ones who lost everything were not lost to him”?

paintings.title: amen
paintings.epigraph: “Amen! May Yahweh do so.”
paintings.poem:
another prophet
stood up in the temple:
two years,
and it'll all be over.

he took the wooden yoke
off Jeremiah's neck
and broke it.

and Jeremiah said:
amen.
may the Lord do so.

he wanted it
to be true.

a true prophet
doesn't love
being right
about the hard things.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the quiet centerpiece of “amen” in this painting (Jeremiah 28:1–11)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: build houses
paintings.epigraph: “Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.”
paintings.poem:
a letter came
all the way from Jerusalem.

they must have hoped
it said:
pack your things.

it said:
build houses.
plant gardens.
eat what grows.
have weddings.
hold babies.

you're going to be here
a while.

it wasn't giving up.

it was God saying
even here,
live.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the quiet centerpiece of “build houses”: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “it was God saying even here, live”?

paintings.title: the peace of the city
paintings.epigraph: “Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Y ahweh for it”
paintings.poem:
pray for the city,
he wrote.

not the old one.
the new one.

the one with the strange gods
and the strange language
and the walls
you didn't choose.

seek its peace.

because in its peace
you will find
your own.

you can't bless a place
and stay
a stranger in it
forever.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “the peace of the city” (Jeremiah 29:7) from “pray for the city, he wrote” to “you can't bless a place and stay a stranger in it forever”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: a future and a hope
paintings.epigraph: “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.”
paintings.poem:
seventy years,
the letter said.

not two.
seventy.

many of them
wouldn't live to see it.

and still:
i know the thoughts i think toward you.
peace, not harm.
a future.
a hope.

you'll seek me with your whole heart
and find me.

a hope
long enough
for your children too.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “a future and a hope” (Jeremiah 29:10–13) arrives at: “a hope long enough for your children too.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: everlasting
paintings.epigraph: “I have loved you with an everlasting love.”
paintings.poem:
after everything—
the broken cisterns,
the belt in the rock,
the long road away—

this:

i have loved you
with an everlasting love.

i'll build you again.

you'll pick up your tambourines.
you'll go out dancing.

the love
didn't start
because you got it right.

so it won't stop
because you didn't.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Jeremiah 31:3–4: “so it won't stop because you didn't”?

paintings.title: with weeping
paintings.epigraph: “They will come with weeping. I will lead them with petitions.”
paintings.poem:
they'll come home
crying.

not marching.
not singing yet.

the blind ones,
the limping ones,
the mothers
with babies on the way.

i'll walk them
by rivers of water,
on a straight road
where no one trips.

he doesn't wait
for the tears to stop
before he brings them.

the tears
come too.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the moving water: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “he doesn't wait for the tears to stop before he brings them. the tears come too”?

paintings.title: Rachel
paintings.epigraph: “There is hope for your latter end”
paintings.poem:
a voice in Ramah.
weeping.
a mother
who won't be comforted.

and God doesn't tell her
to stop.

he says:
your work
will be rewarded.

they will come back.

there is hope
for what comes after.

he doesn't hurry her grief.
he sets a door
at the end of it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “he sets a door at the end of it.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Jeremiah 31:15–17 right now?

paintings.title: sweet
paintings.epigraph: “On this I awakened, and saw; and my sleep was sweet to me.”
paintings.poem:
after all the hard words,
a dream of comfort—

and he woke up
and said:

my sleep
was sweet.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Jeremiah 31:25–26, grace meets us right beside the quiet centerpiece of “sweet”: how does the closing thought—“after all the hard words, a dream of comfort— and he woke up and said: my sleep was sweet”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: new covenant
paintings.epigraph: “I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.”
paintings.poem:
the old covenant
was carved on stone.
they broke it.

so God said:
a new one.
not on tablets this time.
i'll write it
on their hearts.

they'll all know me,
the least to the greatest.

and the last line
is the best:

i will forgive,
and i will not
remember.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “new covenant” (Jeremiah 31:31–34) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“and the last line is the best: i will forgive, and i will not remember”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: a field in Anathoth
paintings.epigraph: “Houses and fields and vineyards will yet again be bought in this land.”
paintings.poem:
the army was outside the walls.
the prophet was locked in the guard's court.

and his cousin came
with a strange request:
buy my field.

so he did.
seventeen shekels of silver,
weighed out.
the deed signed and sealed,
witnesses watching,
the papers put in a clay jar
to last.

who buys land
when the city is about to fall?

someone who believes
there will be
a morning after.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Jeremiah 32:6–15)—where in your own home or work today does “someone who believes there will be a morning after” ring true?

paintings.title: too hard
paintings.epigraph: “There is nothing too hard for you.”
paintings.poem:
you made the heavens,
he prayed.
there is nothing
too hard for you.

and then, honestly:
but you told me
to buy a field.
and the city
is falling.

God answered
with his own words
handed back:

i am the God
of all flesh.

is anything
too hard
for me?
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “is anything too hard for me?.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: again
paintings.epigraph: “the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride”
paintings.poem:
the streets
had gone quiet.

no millstones.
no lamps.
no weddings.

and God said:
again.

in this very place,
the one you call empty—

a bride laughing.
a groom's voice.
people bringing thanks
to his house

and singing
his love endures
forever.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “the streets had gone quiet.” Looking through the lens of Jeremiah 33:10–11, what does it mean to discover that “people bringing thanks to his house and singing his love endures forever”?

paintings.title: the winter house
paintings.epigraph: “there was a fire in the brazier burning before him.”
paintings.poem:
winter.
the king by the fire.
a servant reads
the prophet's scroll aloud.

three or four leaves,
and the king
cuts them off
and drops them in the coals.

then three or four more,
until the whole thing
is gone.

nobody is afraid.

just a warm room
and a man
who didn't want to hear.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the warmth of the fire in this painting (Jeremiah 36:20–24)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: another scroll
paintings.epigraph: “Take again another scroll”
paintings.poem:
the king burned it.

so God said:
take another scroll.

and Baruch sat down
with his pen
and wrote it
all again.

every word.
and more.

you can burn
the page.

you can't burn
the one
who said it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the unrolled parchment: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “you can't burn the one who said it”?

paintings.title: the bakers’ street
paintings.epigraph: “They gave him daily a loaf of bread out of the bakers’ street, until all the bread in the city was gone.”
paintings.poem:
in the guard's court
they gave him
one loaf a day
from the bakers' street.

one loaf.
every day.

until there was
no bread left
in the city.

sometimes faithfulness
looks like this:

enough
for today.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “the bakers’ street” (Jeremiah 37:16–21) from “in the guard's court they gave him one loaf a day from the bakers' street” to “sometimes faithfulness looks like this: enough for today”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: rags and ropes
paintings.epigraph: “Now put these rags and worn-out garments under your armpits under the cords.”
paintings.poem:
they let him down
into the cistern with ropes.
no water.
just mud.
and he sank.

then Ebedmelech the Ethiopian
went to the king
and spoke up for him.

he came back with men,
ropes,
and something else:
old rags.
worn-out clothes.

courage
brought the ropes.

kindness
remembered the rags.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “rags and ropes” (Jeremiah 38:6–13) arrives at: “kindness remembered the rags.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: because you trusted
paintings.epigraph: “because you have put your trust in me”
paintings.poem:
the city fell.

and God
remembered
the man with the rags.

tell Ebedmelech,
he said:
i will rescue you.
you will come through this alive.

not because he was important.
not because he was from here.

because
he trusted me.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Jeremiah 39:15–18: “not because he was important. because he trusted me”?

paintings.title: wherever you go
paintings.epigraph: “I will let you escape with your life wherever you go.”
paintings.poem:
Baruch was tired.
sorrow on top of sorrow,
he said.
i can't rest.

God didn't promise him
greatness.

don't go looking for great things,
he said.

but i'll give you
your life,
wherever you go.

it sounds small.

it's the kind of gift
that fits in a traveler's bag
and lasts
the whole road.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the quiet centerpiece of “wherever you go”: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “it's the kind of gift that fits in a traveler's bag and lasts the whole road”?

paintings.title: pomegranates
paintings.epigraph: “with network and pomegranates on the capital all around”
paintings.poem:
near the end,
an inventory.

pots. shovels.
lampstands. bowls.
the great bronze pillars
with pomegranates
all around the tops.

carried off
to Babylon.

sometimes grief
sounds like that—
counting
what was beautiful

so it won't be
forgotten.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “sometimes grief sounds like that— counting what was beautiful so it won't be forgotten.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Jeremiah 52:17–23 right now?

paintings.title: he spoke kindly
paintings.epigraph: “He spoke kindly to him”
paintings.poem:
thirty-seven years
a captive.

then one day
a new king
opened the door.

he spoke kindly to him.
gave him new clothes.
a seat at the table.
bread every day
for the rest of his life.

that's how Jeremiah ends.

not with the fire.

with a door
opening,
a kind word,
and bread.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Jeremiah 52:31–34, grace meets us right beside the table set before you: how does the closing thought—“with a door opening, a kind word, and bread”—steady your footing for the road ahead?
